lead: This unit is the energy accounting of thermodynamics: heat, work and stored energy are tied together by one balance that holds for every process and every cycle. By the end you can apply the first law to a closed system, a steady-flow device and a vessel being filled or emptied, compute work and heat for isothermal, adiabatic and polytropic paths, and say clearly what the first law cannot tell you.
about: The unit builds one balance and then widens its reach. It starts with the first law for a closed system, for a process and for a cycle, with the forms of energy and moving boundary work. Internal energy and enthalpy come next, then the two specific heats of a gas and the relation between them. These give work, heat and end temperature for isothermal, adiabatic and polytropic paths. The perpetual motion machine of the first kind is the machine the law rules out. The balance is then extended to steady-flow devices (turbines, nozzles, compressors, throttles, heat exchangers) and to unsteady flow, filling and emptying vessels. The unit closes with the questions the first law leaves open, which the second law answers.

chapters.idea: Energy is conserved: for a closed system the heat added minus the work done equals the change in internal energy, and over a complete cycle the net heat equals the net work.
chapters.depth: Statement in words, then the two forms. Cycle form: ∮δQ = ∮δW, so the net area inside the p-V loop is the net work. Process form: Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = U₂ − U₁, with Q positive when added to the system and W positive when done by the system. Differential form: δQ − δW = dU. Explain that Q and W depend on the path while U depends only on the end states, using two different paths between the same states. State the corollaries: the energy of an isolated system is constant, and a cycle cannot produce net work without net heat. Some syllabi call the process form 'first law applied to a process' and these 'corollaries of the first law'; a control mass is the same thing as a closed system. Work out displacement work as the area under the process curve on a p-V diagram, taken from Unit 1.

figure.title: Energy balance for a closed system
figure.aria: Heat enters a closed system, the system's internal energy changes, and work leaves the system.

chapters.example: A gas in a piston-cylinder device receives 80 kJ of heat and does 30 kJ of work as it goes from state 1 to state 2. Find the change in internal energy. Then the gas is brought back to state 1 by a path in which 20 kJ of work is done on the gas; find the heat transfer. Solution: ΔU = Q − W = 80 − 30 = 50 kJ, so U₂ − U₁ = 50 kJ. For the return path U₁ − U₂ = −50 kJ and W = −20 kJ, so Q = ΔU + W = −50 − 20 = −70 kJ. The gas rejects 70 kJ of heat. Over the whole cycle Q_net = 80 − 70 = 10 kJ and W_net = 30 − 20 = 10 kJ, equal as the cycle form requires.
chapters.trap: Treating Q or W as properties of the state. Only U is a property; writing 'the heat of state 2' is wrong. The other slip is the sign of work when work is done on the system, or when work is done on the gas.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: system and surroundings, state and path, work and heat with sign convention, displacement work.
chapters.leave: PMM-1 to Chapter 2.5, the steady-flow form to Chapter 2.6, entropy to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Internal energy U is the energy stored inside the matter, and enthalpy H = U + pV is a second state property that bundles in the flow work and appears wherever mass crosses a boundary.
chapters.depth: Microscopic picture of U: kinetic energy of molecules plus potential energy of their forces. U is a state property, an extensive property, measured in kJ, with specific internal energy u in kJ/kg. For an ideal gas u depends on temperature only; state this and use it, without proving it. Define enthalpy H = U + pV, h = u + pv, and show that ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV); for an ideal gas Δ(pV) = mRΔT, so Δh = cpΔT. Explain why it exists: in a flow device the fluid entering carries both its internal energy and the pV work needed to push it in, so the pair always appears together and deserves a name. Warn that 'heat content' is a loose name and enthalpy is not heat. Mention that at constant pressure the heat added equals ΔH, and that latent heat in a phase change is an enthalpy change (used in Unit 5).

figure.title: Enthalpy bundles two terms
figure.aria: Internal energy and flow work are added together to give enthalpy.

chapters.example: 2 kg of air (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K. Find ΔU, ΔH and Δ(pV). Solution: ΔT = 100 K. ΔU = m cv ΔT = 2 × 0.718 × 100 = 143.6 kJ. ΔH = m cp ΔT = 2 × 1.005 × 100 = 201.0 kJ. Δ(pV) = m R ΔT = 2 × 0.287 × 100 = 57.4 kJ. Check: 143.6 + 57.4 = 201.0 kJ, matching ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV).
chapters.trap: Applying an enthalpy formula to a closed rigid tank, where no flow work occurs and the heat at constant volume equals ΔU, not ΔH. The other slip is adding R to cv to get cp when R is in J/kg·K and cv in kJ/kg·K.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for Q − W = ΔU, and Unit 1 for properties and state.
chapters.leave: The proof of cp − cv = R to Chapter 2.3, steam and latent heat values to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Specific heat at constant volume cv is the heat per kg per kelvin that raises internal energy, specific heat at constant pressure cp is the heat per kg per kelvin that raises enthalpy, and for an ideal gas cp − cv = R.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic, so keep it short and formula-centred. Definitions: cv = (∂u/∂T) at constant volume, cp = (∂h/∂T) at constant pressure, units kJ/kg·K. Explain physically why cp > cv: at constant pressure part of the heat becomes work pΔv, so more heat is needed for the same ΔT. Mayer's relation cp − cv = R, and γ = cp/cv. Standard values to quote: monatomic gas γ ≈ 1.67, diatomic gas such as air γ ≈ 1.4, polyatomic gas γ ≈ 1.3; for air cp = 1.005, cv = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. Mention the link to degrees of freedom only in one line. Do not derive cp and cv from kinetic theory in detail.

figure.title: Same temperature rise, different heat
figure.aria: The same temperature rise needs less heat at constant volume than at constant pressure, and the difference is R.

chapters.example: For air, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. Find R and γ, and check R against the molar mass M = 28.97 kg/kmol with the universal gas constant 8.314 kJ/kmol·K. Solution: R = cp − cv = 1.005 − 0.718 = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. γ = cp/cv = 1.005/0.718 = 1.40. Check: R = 8.314/28.97 = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, which agrees.
chapters.trap: Using cp for a closed rigid vessel held at constant volume, which overestimates the heat by a factor γ. Also mixing kJ and J when R is taken as 287 J/kg·K.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for u, h and Δh = cpΔT.
chapters.leave: The use of γ in pV^γ = C to Chapter 2.4; entropy changes of these processes to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A closed-system process that follows pV^n = C has fixed formulas for work and heat, and the value of n selects the process: n = 0 isobaric, n = 1 isothermal, n = γ adiabatic, and n = ∞ isochoric.
chapters.depth: Start from W = ∫p dV with pV^n = C. For n ≠ 1: W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1) = mR(T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1). For n = 1: W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = mRT ln(V₂/V₁), with ΔU = 0 so Q = W. Adiabatic: Q = 0, pV^γ = C, and the gas relations some syllabi call the 'gas equation during an adiabatic process': T₂/T₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = (p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ), with W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(γ−1) = m cv (T₁ − T₂). Isobaric: W = p(V₂ − V₁), Q = m cp ΔT. Isochoric: W = 0, Q = m cv ΔT. Polytropic heat: Q = m cn (T₂ − T₁) with cn = cv (n − γ)/(n − 1). Show each path on a p-V diagram and note that the adiabatic falls more steeply than the isothermal.

figure.aria: Expansion curves from the same starting point, with the adiabatic curve falling below the polytropic and the isothermal curves.

chapters.example: 1 kg of air at 300 K and 100 kPa is compressed to one-eighth of its volume. Find the final pressure, final temperature, work and heat transfer if the process is (a) isothermal and (b) adiabatic. Take R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4. Solution (a): T₂ = 300 K. W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 0.287 × 300 × ln(1/8) = 86.1 × (−2.079) = −179.0 kJ. ΔU = 0, so Q = W = −179.0 kJ: 179 kJ of work goes in and 179 kJ of heat comes out. Solution (b): p₂ = p₁(V₁/V₂)^γ = 100 × 8^1.4 = 1838 kPa. T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = 300 × 8^0.4 = 689.2 K. W = m cv (T₁ − T₂) = 0.718 × (300 − 689.2) = −279.5 kJ, and Q = 0.
chapters.trap: Putting n = 1 into the general expression, which divides by zero. Also using γ when the question gives a polytropic index n, and getting the sign of work wrong in compression.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for Q − W = ΔU, Chapter 2.2 for u depending on T, Chapter 2.3 for γ.
chapters.leave: The same processes in flow devices to Chapter 2.6; their entropy change to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind is a device that would create energy, delivering work with no input or more work than the heat supplied, and the first law forbids it outright.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a named topic, so keep it to one short chapter. Definition of PMM-1 in both forms: a machine producing net work in a cycle with no heat input, and an engine with efficiency above 100 percent. Show that ∮δQ = ∮δW rules both out, since a cycle with Q_net = 0 must have W_net = 0. Contrast with PMM-2 in one line: PMM-2 obeys the first law but breaks the second (Unit 3), so first-law tests cannot reject it. Give the examination wording: a device claims certain input and output; check the energy balance and declare it impossible.

figure.title: Why PMM-1 fails
figure.aria: A machine with no heat input claims a work output, and the cycle energy balance rejects that claim.

chapters.example: An inventor claims a closed-cycle machine that takes in 300 kW of heat and delivers 500 kW of shaft work, with no other energy exchange. Test the claim. Solution: in a cycle ∮δQ = ∮δW, so W_net cannot exceed Q_net. Here the claimed net output is 500 − 300 = 200 kW more than the input, which means 200 kW of energy is created. The claim violates the first law, so the machine is a PMM-1 and cannot exist. A second claim of 250 kW output for 200 kW input gives an efficiency of 250/200 = 1.25, that is 125 percent, which is equally impossible.
chapters.trap: Rejecting a device by saying 'efficiency is too low' instead of checking the first-law balance, or confusing PMM-1 with PMM-2, which does not violate the first law.
chapters.leave: PMM-2, Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: For a steady-flow open system the energy carried in by the fluid, plus heat added, equals the energy carried out plus work done, which gives the steady flow energy equation h₁ + V₁²/2 + gz₁ + q = h₂ + V₂²/2 + gz₂ + w.
chapters.depth: State the assumptions: steady state, uniform properties across inlet and outlet sections, negligible change in the control volume's own energy, and q and w per unit mass. Identify each term: h in kJ/kg, V²/2 in J/kg so divide by 1000, gz in J/kg so divide by 1000. Note that a control volume is an open system and that the mass flow rate ṁ multiplies every term to give kW. Then derive each application from the general equation by striking out terms: nozzle (q = w = 0, so h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2; velocity rises, enthalpy falls), diffuser (the reverse), turbine (neglect KE and PE, w = h₁ − h₂), compressor (w is negative, work input), throttle or expansion valve (q = 0, w = 0, so h₁ = h₂, isenthalpic), boiler and condenser (w = 0, q = h₂ − h₁), heat exchanger, and pump. Mention in one line the uniform-state uniform-flow filling problem, called SSSF and USUF in some syllabi.

figure.title: Steady flow energy balance
figure.aria: Fluid enters with enthalpy, kinetic and potential energy, heat crosses the boundary in and shaft work leaves, and the fluid exits with its own energy terms.

chapters.example: Steam enters an insulated turbine at 2 kg/s with h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg, V₁ = 60 m/s and z₁ = 5 m. It leaves with h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg, V₂ = 150 m/s and z₂ = 0 m. Heat loss from the casing is 20 kJ per kg of steam. Find the power output. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Solution: per kg, w = (h₁ − h₂) + (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 + g(z₁ − z₂)/1000 + q. Here h₁ − h₂ = 600 kJ/kg. (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 = (3600 − 22500)/2000 = −9.45 kJ/kg. g(z₁ − z₂)/1000 = 9.81 × 5/1000 = 0.049 kJ/kg. q = −20 kJ/kg. So w = 600 − 9.45 + 0.049 − 20 = 570.6 kJ/kg, and power = 2 × 570.6 = 1141 kW, about 1.14 MW.
chapters.trap: Dropping the kinetic energy term in a nozzle, where it is the whole point, or keeping it in a turbine where it is small. Also forgetting to divide V²/2 by 1000 before adding it to h in kJ/kg, and getting the sign of w wrong for a compressor.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the energy balance, Chapter 2.2 for enthalpy, Chapter 2.4 for the process paths.
chapters.leave: Entropy generation and isentropic efficiency of these devices to Unit 3 and Unit 4; steam property values to Unit 5; turbines and compressors inside cycles to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The first law counts energy but gives no direction, so it cannot explain why heat flows from hot to cold, why work turns fully into heat but not the reverse, or why a PMM-2 fails.
chapters.depth: List the limitations plainly. First, no direction: both a hot body cooling and a cold body warming on its own balance energy exactly, yet only one happens. Second, no quality: work and heat are equal in joules but not in usefulness, since work converts fully to heat while heat cannot convert fully to work. Third, it accepts impossible machines: an engine with 100 percent efficiency passes the first law. Fourth, it gives no criterion for equilibrium or for spontaneity, and it does not separate reversible from irreversible processes, though both satisfy it. Use two examples of processes that both obey the first law while only one is possible. Close by naming what fills the gap: the second law and entropy in Unit 3, and available and unavailable energy in Unit 4.

figure.title: What the first law leaves open
figure.aria: The first law balances energy both ways round a process and so predicts no direction, which is why the second law is required.

chapters.example: A cup holds 0.2 kg of water at 80 °C in a room at 25 °C. Take the specific heat of water as 4.18 kJ/kg·K. (a) Find the heat the water loses on cooling to room temperature. (b) Show that the reverse process also balances energy, and state which law rules it out. Solution (a): Q = m c ΔT = 0.2 × 4.18 × (80 − 25) = 0.2 × 4.18 × 55 = 46.0 kJ, rejected to the room. (b) The reverse would be the room giving exactly 46.0 kJ back to the cup, raising it from 25 °C to 80 °C, and the energy balance closes perfectly. So the first law permits both directions; the second law, through the increase of entropy, forbids the reverse. That gap is the whole point of this chapter.
chapters.trap: Writing that a process 'violates the first law' when the real objection is direction. A cold cup warming on its own breaks the second law, not the first.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the energy balance and Chapter 2.6 for real devices that still lose usefulness.
chapters.leave: Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, the Carnot cycle and entropy to Unit 3; exergy and second law efficiency to Unit 4.
